chapter_summary:
Welcome to the world of Ethereum, a revolutionary platform that extends the core concepts of blockchain beyond simple cryptocurrency transactions to enable a global, decentralized computer. While Bitcoin introduced the idea of digital scarcity and peer-to-peer electronic cash, Ethereum pioneered the concept of a "world computer" capable of executing arbitrary code in a trustless environment. This distinction is crucial: Bitcoin is primarily a digital currency; Ethereum is a programmable blockchain, a foundation upon which decentralized applications (dApps) can be built. This programmability is largely thanks to its central component, the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM).

The Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is the heart of the Ethereum network, acting as a global, single-instance runtime environment for all smart contracts. Think of the EVM as a massive, decentralized computer that maintains the state of the entire Ethereum blockchain. Every node in the Ethereum network runs an EVM, ensuring that all participants agree on the outcome of every smart contract execution. When a smart contract function is called, the EVM executes its bytecode, updating the state of the blockchain accordingly. This deterministic execution is what makes Ethereum trustless and verifiable: given the same input, the EVM will always produce the same output on every node, guaranteeing consistency across the network. Understanding the EVM is fundamental to grasping how smart contracts operate and interact with the blockchain state.

Ethereum utilizes two primary types of accounts: Externally Owned Accounts (EOAs) and Contract Accounts. An EOA is controlled by a private key, similar to a Bitcoin wallet. It has an Ether balance and can send transactions, including simple Ether transfers or transactions that trigger smart contract execution. Crucially, EOAs cannot execute code directly; they are merely initiators. A Contract Account, on the other hand, does not have a private key and is controlled by the code stored within it. It also has an Ether balance and a nonce (transaction count), but its primary function is to store and execute smart contract code. When an EOA sends a transaction to a Contract Account, the EVM executes the contract's code, which can then perform actions like sending Ether, creating new contracts, or modifying its internal state. This distinction is vital for understanding how value and logic flow through the Ethereum network.

The lifecycle of an Ethereum transaction begins when an EOA signs a transaction with its private key and broadcasts it to the network. This transaction could be a simple Ether transfer to another EOA, or it could be a call to a function within a smart contract. Once broadcast, the transaction enters the "mempool," a waiting area for unconfirmed transactions. Ethereum nodes then pick up these transactions, validate them (checking for correct signature, sufficient balance, etc.), and include them in a block. Miners (or validators in a Proof-of-Stake system) compete to create the next valid block by solving a computational puzzle (or by being chosen based on stake). Once a block containing the transaction is successfully mined and added to the blockchain, the transaction is considered confirmed. The more blocks that are added on top of it, the more "final" the transaction becomes, making it increasingly difficult to revert.

For example, if Alice wants to send 1 Ether to Bob, she would use a wallet application (like MetaMask) to create a transaction. This transaction would specify Bob's address as the recipient, 1 Ether as the value, and her own address as the sender. After signing with her private key, the transaction is sent to an Ethereum node, which then propagates it across the network. Miners pick up this transaction, include it in a block, and once that block is successfully added to the blockchain, Bob's account balance is updated. Similarly, if Alice wanted to interact with a decentralized exchange (DEX) smart contract to swap tokens, her transaction would call a specific function on that contract, and the EVM would execute the contract's code to facilitate the token swap.

A common mistake beginners make is confusing the Ethereum network with the Ether cryptocurrency. Ether (ETH) is the native cryptocurrency of the Ethereum network, used to pay for transaction fees (gas) and as a store of value. Ethereum, however, is the underlying blockchain platform that enables smart contracts and dApps. Another pitfall is underestimating the importance of gas. Every operation on the EVM costs gas, which is paid in Ether. If a transaction doesn't include enough gas, it will fail, but you will still pay for the gas consumed up to the point of failure. This is a crucial safety mechanism to prevent malicious or inefficient code from consuming infinite computational resources. Always ensure your transactions have an adequate gas limit, but don't overpay by setting an excessively high gas price unless absolutely necessary for urgent transactions.

screens.title: Introduction to Ethereum
screens.subtitle: From digital money to a global, programmable computer

narration.text: Welcome — in this lesson you will build a clear mental model of what Ethereum is and why it matters. Ethereum takes the blockchain idea beyond cryptocurrency and becomes a platform that runs code in a trustless way. That ability to execute smart contracts on a shared global state is what allows decentralized applications, automated financial services, and tokenized assets to exist without a central operator. You will see why the Ethereum Virtual Machine is described as a decentralized runtime, how externally owned accounts differ from contract accounts, and what happens to a transaction from your wallet until it is confirmed in a block. I will also point out common beginner mistakes, like confusing Ether the currency with Ethereum the platform, and explain gas so you know why transactions can fail even when you have enough funds. By the end of this chapter you should be able to read a transaction on a block explorer, identify whether an address is a user or a contract, and explain why deterministic execution across many nodes makes smart contracts verifiable. Consider right now: what decentralized application would you want to power with predictable, on‑chain logic?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Ethereum is a programmable blockchain: Ether is its currency, and the EVM is the shared runtime that executes smart contract logic deterministically for all nodes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will gain in this chapter

narration.text: These four objectives will shape what you can do after this chapter. First, you will be able to explain how Ethereum differs from Bitcoin, focusing on programmability and decentralized applications rather than purely a ledger for money. Second, you will be able to describe the EVM: what it is, why it runs the same code on every node, and why deterministic execution matters for trustless systems. Third, you will learn to tell Externally Owned Accounts apart from Contract Accounts, including the roles of private keys, code storage, and how each can hold Ether. Fourth, you will trace a transaction from signing to confirmation, including the mempool stage, validation checks, and how inclusion in a block leads to finality. For each objective, you'll see a short mnemonic or visual to help the idea stick, and a verified competency milestone points to a concrete artifact you can produce, like a written explanation or a block explorer snapshot.

screens.title: Ethereum vs Bitcoin
screens.subtitle: Why Ethereum is a programmable platform and Bitcoin is primarily a digital currency

narration.text: Begin with a clear distinction: Bitcoin was designed as a ledger for value transfer, with scripting intentionally limited for safety and simplicity. Ethereum was designed to run general-purpose code on a shared state, enabling decentralized applications that can hold logic and state on-chain. This matters because it changes the system's goals. Bitcoin focuses on secure, censorship-resistant transfers of value. Ethereum focuses on predictable execution of programs that can coordinate financial and organizational logic. Concrete example: a simple Bitcoin transaction moves funds from Alice to Bob and ends; an Ethereum transaction can call a smart contract that swaps tokens, updates balances, emits events, and creates new contracts, all in one atomic execution. A frequent misconception is thinking both networks are interchangeable for dApps: they are not. Ethereum's EVM, accounts model, and gas system are purpose-built for reproducible computation across nodes. That same complexity brings trade-offs: more surface for bugs and higher operational needs like gas management. Takeaway: if your goal is programmable, verifiable logic on-chain, Ethereum provides primitives Bitcoin does not. Ask yourself: does your application need stateful, verifiable execution, or simple, minimal value transfer?

keyIdea.title: Distinction
keyIdea.text: Bitcoin = ledger for value transfer; Ethereum = programmable state and execution environment for decentralized applications.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Ethereum vs Bitcoin
Core Claim

Different design goals

Bitcoin prioritizes secure value transfer with minimal scripting. Ethereum prioritizes deterministic execution of arbitrary programs on a shared blockchain state.

Bitcoin example

Send 1 BTC from Alice to Bob; ledger updates and transaction is final.

Ethereum example

Call a DEX smart contract to swap tokens; the contract executes code and updates multiple balances atomically.

Common misconception

Not all blockchains are equally suited for on‑chain programs; architecture and gas change what you can build.

Comparison
Scope
Bitcoin: value transfer. Ethereum: value + computation.
Programming model
Bitcoin: limited scripts. Ethereum: Turing‑complete EVM bytecode executed by nodes.
Costs
Bitcoin: transaction fee. Ethereum: gas for each operation; gas limits control execution.
Key Takeaway

Choose Ethereum when you need shared, verifiable program execution; choose Bitcoin for minimal, robust value transfer.

screens.title: The Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)
screens.subtitle: A deterministic, global runtime for smart contract bytecode

narration.text: The Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM, is the runtime that executes smart contract bytecode and produces changes to blockchain state. Think of it as a decentralized single-instance computer replicated across every full node. When you call a smart contract function, the EVM on every validating node executes the same bytecode with the same inputs, and all nodes must arrive at the same resulting state. This deterministic execution is the foundation of trustlessness: anyone can verify that the same code with the same inputs yields the same outputs. A concrete example: a token transfer function subtracts and adds balances; the EVM executes arithmetic and storage writes and returns a new state visible to all nodes. A common misconception is expecting the EVM to be like a standard server process — instead it is constrained: operations cost gas, and there is no notion of hidden background computation. Also, because every node runs the same execution, bugs or inefficiencies in contracts affect the entire network. Key takeaway: the EVM provides predictable, auditable execution, but it imposes execution costs and immutable behavior once deployed.

keyIdea.title: EVM in one line
keyIdea.text: A replicated, deterministic runtime that executes smart contract bytecode and updates the shared Ethereum state.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › EVM
Definition

Ethereum Virtual Machine

A replicated runtime that executes smart contract bytecode deterministically on every full node, producing identical state transitions.

Concrete example

A token contract's transfer function updates two balances and emits an event; the EVM makes the same updates on every node.

Why determinism matters

Determinism ensures consensus: nodes can independently verify that the same code and inputs produce the same outputs.

Common misconception

The EVM is not a cloud server; operations cost gas and every step is visible in the shared state.

Anatomy
Inputs
Transaction data, caller address, and current state.
Processing
Bytecode execution steps charged in gas.
Outputs
State updates, logs, and return data.
Key Takeaway

EVM makes smart contracts auditable and verifiable, but imposes gas costs for every operation.

screens.title: Account Types: EOAs vs Contract Accounts
screens.subtitle: Who controls an account, and how does code run on-chain?

narration.text: Ethereum has two primary account types with different control models. An Externally Owned Account, or EOA, is controlled by a private key. A person or wallet signs a transaction from an EOA and that signed transaction is what can initiate state changes. EOAs have a balance and a nonce but do not contain executable code. A Contract Account, in contrast, contains deployed bytecode and is controlled by that code rather than a private key. Contract Accounts can hold Ether, maintain internal storage, and when they receive a transaction the EVM executes their code. Concrete example: Alice uses her EOA and MetaMask to sign a transaction calling a DEX contract; the DEX contract account then runs token swap logic. A common misconception is expecting a contract account to 'decide' to send transactions itself — it cannot initiate actions without a transaction from an EOA or another contract during execution. Key takeaway: EOAs initiate, contract accounts respond and execute stored logic. Ask yourself: when you see an address on a block explorer, which clues tell you if it is a contract or an EOA?

keyIdea.title: Account model
keyIdea.text: EOAs are user-controlled via private keys and initiate transactions; Contract Accounts hold code and execute when called by transactions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Account Types
Externally Owned Account

EOA — controlled by a private key

Signs transactions, sends Ether, and calls contracts. Has balance and nonce but no code.

Example

Alice signs a transaction in her wallet to call a DEX swap.

Misconception

An EOA cannot execute code on its own; it only signs and sends transactions.

Contract Account

Contract — controlled by deployed code

Holds bytecode and storage. Executes when called and can send Ether or create other contracts during execution.

Example

A token contract transfers balances and emits events when invoked by a transaction.

Key takeaway

Contracts act on input; EOAs provide signed input. Neither can spontaneously create a signed transaction outside execution flow.

screens.title: Transaction Lifecycle
screens.subtitle: From private key signing to block confirmation

narration.text: A transaction on Ethereum follows a clear lifecycle with distinct stages. First, an Externally Owned Account constructs and signs a transaction, specifying recipient, value, data, gasLimit, and gasPrice. Second, the signed transaction is broadcast to nodes and enters the mempool — a waiting area of unconfirmed transactions. Third, nodes pick up transactions from the mempool, validate signatures and balances, and include valid transactions in candidate blocks. Fourth, a miner or validator produces a block containing the transaction; when the block is accepted the transaction is included and its effects apply to the canonical state. Finally, confirmations accumulate as more blocks build on top, increasing finality. Concrete example: Alice signs a transfer to Bob, the transaction stays in the mempool for several blocks, then is mined and her balance decreases while Bob's increases. A common misconception is that inclusion in a single block is absolute finality; in practice, more confirmations make reversion exponentially harder. Takeaway: follow these stages when debugging failed transactions — check signature, gas, mempool presence, and block inclusion to find where the issue occurred. Transaction Lifecycle means sign → broadcast → mempool → validate → include in block → confirmations increase finality.. In practical terms, from private key signing to block confirmation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle steps
keyIdea.text: Sign → Broadcast → Mempool → Validate → Include in block → Confirmations increase finality.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Transaction Lifecycle
Process Flow

Transaction lifecycle steps

1
Sign
EOA signs transaction with private key; transaction includes gasLimit and gasPrice.
2
Broadcast to mempool
Nodes receive and relay the transaction; it waits for inclusion.
3
Validate & include
Validators check signature, nonce, and balance then include it in a block.
4
Confirmations
As new blocks are added, the transaction becomes more final and harder to revert.
Supporting notes
  • Validation checks: signature, nonce ordering, and sufficient balance for value plus gas limit.
  • Mempool: not ordered globally; miners pick by fee and local policy.
  • Failure: if gas runs out, state reverts and gas is consumed up to failure point.
Key Takeaway

To debug a transaction, inspect signature, nonce, gas, mempool presence, and block inclusion.

screens.title: Mempool and Transaction Validation
screens.subtitle: Why transactions wait, how nodes validate them, and common failure reasons

narration.text: The mempool is a transient queue of unconfirmed transactions that nodes store and share. When you broadcast a signed transaction it lands in the mempool while waiting to be validated and included in a block. Nodes validate transactions by checking the signature, that the nonce matches the sender's next expected nonce, and that the sender has enough Ether to cover value plus gasLimit times gasPrice. A concrete scenario: you submit a contract call but set a gasLimit that is too low for the execution path. Validators will still accept the transaction into the mempool, but when miners execute it while assembling a block the transaction may run out of gas and fail — the state reverts but gas is consumed. A common misconception is assuming a transaction will never be accepted into mempool without correct gas; mempools often accept many transactions but the execution outcome is only known when a miner runs the EVM. Takeaway: checking mempool presence, gasLimit, and nonce are often the fastest ways to diagnose why a transaction is delayed or failing. Ask: is the transaction stuck because of low fee, wrong nonce, or insufficient gas?

keyIdea.title: Mempool role
keyIdea.text: Mempool holds unconfirmed transactions; nodes validate signatures, nonces, and balance before miners include transactions in blocks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Mempool & Validation
Concept

Mempool behavior and validation checks

Transactions wait in the mempool until miners choose them. Nodes perform early validation for signature, nonce, and balance before relaying.

Example

Low gasLimit on a contract call causes execution to run out of gas during mining; the call fails but gas consumed is not returned.

Checks before inclusion

Signature validity, correct nonce sequence, and sufficient balance for value plus potential gas costs.

Misconception

Mempool acceptance does not guarantee success; execution outcome is only finalized when the block is produced and executed.

Quick checklist
  • Signature: correct signing key?
  • Nonce: does it match the sender's next expected value?
  • Gas: gasLimit sufficient for contract execution?
  • Fee: gasPrice competitive for inclusion?
Key Takeaway

When debugging, confirm mempool visibility, nonce order, and correct gas settings before looking deeper into contract logic.

screens.title: Gas Mechanics and Fee Calculation
screens.subtitle: How gasUsed, gasLimit, and gasPrice determine transaction fees

narration.text: Gas measures the computational effort of EVM operations. When creating a transaction you set a gasLimit and a gasPrice. GasUsed is the actual amount consumed during execution. The fee you pay equals gasUsed multiplied by gasPrice. Concrete example from the chapter: Alice sets gasLimit 100,000 and gasPrice 20 Gwei, but the function consumes 80,000 gas. The fee equals 80,000 times 20 Gwei, which converts to 0.0016 Ether; the unused 20,000 gas is not charged and is effectively refunded. A common mistake is believing unused gas is simply returned as Ether in a second transaction; instead the protocol refunds unused gas from the preauthorized amount. Another mistake is setting an overly low gasLimit, which causes the transaction to run out of gas and revert while still charging consumed gas. Practical guidance: set a gasLimit slightly above your expected worst case, and set a competitive gasPrice when you need faster inclusion. Now let’s inspect a short code-like example that shows the fee calculation and a sample transaction structure so you can compute fees quickly when analyzing a block explorer entry. Gas Mechanics and Fee Calculation means transaction fee = gasused × gasprice. gaslimit sets a maximum; unused gas is refunded, but consumed gas is paid even on failure.. In practical terms, how gasused, gaslimit, and gasprice determine transaction fees. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Gas formula
keyIdea.text: Transaction fee = gasUsed × gasPrice. gasLimit sets a maximum; unused gas is refunded, but consumed gas is paid even on failure.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Gas Mechanics
Formula

Fee calculation

Fee is gasUsed multiplied by gasPrice; gasLimit is your maximum willingness to spend.

Transaction example:
{
  from: "0xAlice",
  to: "0xBob",
  value: 1 ETH,
  gasLimit: 100000,
  gasPrice: 20 Gwei
}

Execution consumes: gasUsed = 80000
Fee = 80000 * 20 Gwei = 1,600,000 Gwei = 0.0016 ETH
Notes & pitfalls
  • Low gasLimit: causes revert and still consumes gas up to failure.
  • Unused gas: refunded automatically; you only pay gasUsed.
  • Urgency: higher gasPrice increases the likelihood of faster inclusion.
Quick calculation

Multiply gasUsed by gasPrice and convert units carefully between Gwei and Ether when comparing fees.

screens.title: Contract Interactions and Internal Transactions
screens.subtitle: How contracts call other contracts and produce internal transfers

narration.text: Contracts interact with each other during execution, producing what are commonly called internal transactions. When a transaction calls a contract function, that contract can call other contracts, send Ether, or create new contracts. These internal actions do not contain separate signed transactions; they are executed as part of the originating transaction and are visible as internal traces on block explorers. Concrete example: Alice calls a DeFi router that executes a series of swaps across multiple token contracts; the router contract will call token contracts and change balances, producing internal transfer traces. A common misconception is thinking every on-chain transfer is represented by a top-level transaction; internal transfers can move funds without new top-level signatures. Another important point: because internal actions run within the original EVM execution context, they share the same gas and failure semantics — if an internal call runs out of gas or reverts without handling, it can cause the entire originating transaction to revert unless explicitly handled. Takeaway: when auditing or debugging, inspect internal transactions and traces to fully understand the effects of a contract call. Contract Interactions and Internal Transactions means contract calls can trigger other contracts and internal transfers; these are executed within the original transaction and share its gas context.. In practical terms, how contracts call other contracts and produce internal transfers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Internal actions
keyIdea.text: Contract calls can trigger other contracts and internal transfers; these are executed within the original transaction and share its gas context.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Contract Interactions
Architecture

Internal transactions and call chains

A top-level transaction can invoke a contract which then calls other contracts. These internal invocations are part of the same execution and are traced rather than signed separately.

Example

A DEX router receives a swap request and calls multiple token contracts to perform transfers and adjust balances internally.

Misconception

Internal transfers are not separate signed transactions; they are traces produced during contract execution.

Audit tips
  1. Check internal traces for transfers and token approvals.
  2. Confirm gas usage across nested calls to estimate cost.
  3. Look for unhandled reverts in internal calls that could cause overall failure.
Key Takeaway

Internal actions reveal the full behavior of a contract call; inspect traces to see all state changes that occurred.

screens.title: Ethereum Network Components
screens.subtitle: Nodes, clients, and the peer-to-peer layer that keep the chain in sync

narration.text: The Ethereum network is composed of nodes running client software, connected by a peer-to-peer layer that propagates transactions and blocks. A node can be a full node that validates blocks and runs the EVM, or a light node that relies on other nodes for full data. Clients implement the protocol rules and provide the EVM runtime; different client implementations increase resilience if one has a bug. The peer-to-peer layer handles discovery and message relaying, moving signed transactions into mempools across many peers. Concrete example: when you broadcast a signed transaction from your wallet, it reaches a local node which relays it to its peers; those peers propagate it further until miners see it and include it in a block. A common misconception is assuming a single global ordering exists before block inclusion — mempool ordering is local, and miners see different transaction pools. Takeaway: understanding nodes and clients helps you reason about propagation delays, mempool inconsistencies, and how client diversity improves network security. Ethereum Network Components means client software runs the evm and validates blocks; the peer-to-peer layer shares transactions and blocks across nodes to reach consensus.. In practical terms, nodes, clients, and the peer-to-peer layer that keep the chain in sync. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Network anatomy
keyIdea.text: Client software runs the EVM and validates blocks; the peer-to-peer layer shares transactions and blocks across nodes to reach consensus.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Network Components
Core Components

Nodes, clients, and the peer-to-peer layer

Clients implement protocol rules and the EVM. Nodes run clients, maintain state, and relay messages via the P2P layer to reach consensus across the network.

Node types

Full nodes validate and execute EVM code; light nodes rely on full nodes for heavy lifting.

Clients

Different implementations increase robustness; each enforces consensus rules and runs the EVM.

Peer-to-peer

Handles discovery and relaying; mempool contents vary by peer, causing local differences until blocks unify state.

Practical note

When debugging delays, consider peer connectivity and client implementation differences as potential causes of different mempool views.

Key Takeaway

Node and client architecture shapes propagation and resilience; diverse clients and healthy peer connections strengthen the network.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Exploring Accounts and Transactions
screens.subtitle: Use a block explorer to identify EOAs vs Contract Accounts and analyze transaction details

narration.text: The hands-on activity asks you to use a block explorer to compare EOAs and Contract Accounts and inspect transaction records. Begin by finding a likely EOA — look for addresses with many simple outgoing Ether transfers and no contract tab. Then find a Contract Account such as a popular token or protocol; contract pages often include a 'Contract' label and verified source. For the EOA, identify one simple Ether transfer and one contract interaction, noting the transaction hash, method, value, and gas used. For the Contract Account, look for internal transactions and calls from many distinct addresses. A concrete walkthrough: search for a token contract, open its transactions, and note an incoming call that triggered an internal transfer; then open the trace to see the sequence of internal calls. Common pitfalls: confusing contract-created transactions with signing actions — only EOAs create signed top-level transactions. The takeaway is practical: by comparing pages you will learn to tell account types apart and interpret the method and gas fields when diagnosing behavior. Hands-on Activity: Exploring Accounts and Transactions means use a block explorer to identify eoas and contracts, and collect transaction details to explain their behavior and gas usage.. In practical terms, use a block explorer to identify eoas vs contract accounts and analyze transaction details. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Use a block explorer to identify EOAs and contracts, and collect transaction details to explain their behavior and gas usage.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Hands-on Activity
Activity

Exploring account pages and transactions

Follow the activity template to identify an EOA and a Contract Account, then record example transactions and observations for each.

EOA checklist
  • Look for direct ETH transfers and a transactions list without a contract tab.
  • Record a simple transfer: Txn Hash, Method, Value, Gas Used.
Contract checklist
  • Find the 'Contract' label or verified code, inspect internal transactions and traces.
  • Record incoming calls and any internal transfers triggered.
Reflection

Note visual differences: contract pages often show source and internal transactions; EOAs show straightforward transfer histories.

Key Takeaway

Real-world inspection of account pages reinforces how EOAs initiate actions and contracts execute logic visible in internal traces.

narration.text: Here are the condensed core concepts to keep in mind. The Ethereum Virtual Machine is the replicated, deterministic runtime that executes smart contract bytecode and updates the shared state. Externally Owned Accounts are controlled by private keys and sign transactions; they initiate actions but do not contain executable code. Contract Accounts are controlled by their deployed code, hold state, and execute when called. Together, these concepts underlie how dApps function on Ethereum. Practice identifying these elements on a block explorer and explaining how they relate to transaction behavior and gas consumption. Retaining these definitions will make it easier to read transaction traces and reason about failure modes. narration.text: A few operational terms you should remember will help you read transactions and debug issues. Transaction Lifecycle describes signing, mempool, validation, inclusion in a block, and confirmations. The mempool is the waiting area for unconfirmed transactions; it is local to nodes and can show different views before block inclusion. Gas is the unit of computational effort; gasUsed times gasPrice yields the fee you pay, while gasLimit is the maximum gas you authorize. These terms let you explain why a transaction failed, why fees changed, or why propagation was slow. Practice applying these definitions when you inspect transaction details in the hands-on activity. To solidify learning, try explaining the fee calculation and mempool behavior aloud as if teaching a peer.
